interest: This docket sheet is particularly interesting for revealing early 1930s cultural and municipal diplomacy between the United States and Japan, specifically the interest of high-ranking Japanese officials like Count Makino Nobuaki in the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts as a potential model for the post-1923 earthquake beautification and city planning of Tokyo. It also documents how elite private networks—spanning Chicago financiers, the State Department, Count Kabayama, and the Iwasaki zaibatsu family—facilitated private art tourism for prominent Americans, while tracking the transition toward heightened geopolitical vigilance as travelers inquired whether to cancel trips in mid-1937.
overview: This file comprises the Department of State's two-page docket sheet ('List of Papers') for decimal file 894.403 (Social Matters: Japan - Fine Arts), recording official despatches, letters, telegrams, and memoranda generated between 1930 and 1938. The indexed records document inquiries initiated by U.S. Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. on behalf of Count Makino Nobuaki (Lord Privy Seal of Japan) regarding the functions and regulatory powers of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in Washington to inform the urban planning and beautification of Tokyo; the disposition of a two-volume Japanese art catalogue referred to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck; letters of introduction and travel advisories for the Misses Wyatt (arranged through Dr. Walter Lichtenstein of the First National Bank of Chicago) seeking to visit private art collections in Tokyo, notably that of Baron Iwasaki; and an offer of a Japanese art collection to the Smithsonian Institution.

subfiles.summary: This two-page docket sheet registers official records filed under State Department classification 894.403 from April 1930 through February 1938. It records despatches and letters concerning inquiries by Count Makino Nobuaki and Ambassador William R. Castle into the powers and duties of the Washington Commission of Fine Arts under Charles Moore for application to the urban development of Tokyo. The entries also trace departmental actions concerning a two-volume Japanese art catalogue handled by Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, introductions for the Misses Wyatt to view private art collections including Baron Iwasaki's via Count Kabayama, Department travel advice regarding Japan in July 1937, and an offer of Japanese artwork to the Smithsonian Institution.
